data.current_description:
**ASYNCHRONOUS.** Returns 202 immediately with a run whose `status` is `running` — nothing has been searched yet. Poll `GET /v1/discoveries/{runId}` until `settledAt` is non-null, then read the events that stand for its scope with `GET /v1/events?discoveryRunId={runId}`. `settledAt` is set when the run is final — searched AND every event written — and `status` reads `completed` or `failed` at the same instant. `candidatesScreened`, `candidatesMatched` and `eventsNew` are frozen execution counters; the scoped event page holds everything this run wrote — including events dated outside the lookback, as a job change dated by its start month can be — plus matching canonical events written by earlier runs.

**Re-running an identical discovery is safe.** Results deduplicate against everything already in the workspace, so the same accounts/signals/lookback typically returns `eventsNew: 0` the second time and creates no duplicate events. That is success.

**Idempotency:** send `Idempotency-Key` on every call you might retry. Repeating the same key with the byte-identical body returns the ORIGINAL run with the same `id`, without starting another search, but with its CURRENT state, not a frozen copy: if the original has since completed, the replay shows `status: completed` and real counts. The same key with a DIFFERENT body is a 409. Keys are not scoped to a time window in this version.

**A 202 does not guarantee events will follow.** If none of the requested accounts are eligible — every account must be assigned to a user, which accounts created via `POST /v1/accounts` always are — the run still returns 202 and then immediately reads `status: completed`, `eventsNew: 0`, with `error` explaining why. This is the single most likely way a first-time caller sees "no events": check `error` before assuming discovery is still running or that your signals match nothing.

You can use new accounts and signal keys immediately. Poll the same run until `settledAt` is set.

Public REST and MCP usage is recorded without daily usage caps, workspace quota cutoffs or lookup quotas for now. Workspace request pacing still applies. **People:** by default (`people: "none"`) a run adds no people to your workspace — its events come back with `people: []`. A `job_change` event still names the person who changed jobs; add them with `POST /v1/people` if you want them. Send `people: "add"` to have the people who matter to each event added to your workspace and listed on it.

Read `blockedSignals` before reporting an empty result. These outcomes apply to every signal type, including `news`. While a run is active, keep polling the same run. `account_not_ready` means Trayo could not search the account this time. After the run settles, retry the affected account IDs. `company_not_found` means Trayo could not identify the company from the supplied details. For `company_not_found`, check the named accounts before starting another discovery. If an identity is wrong, send the correct `linkedinHandle` with `trayo_update_account` over MCP, or with `PATCH /v1/accounts/{id}` and a workspace API key over REST. When no handle is known, send a corrected website `url` instead. Both need `accounts:write`. `trayo_update_account` also reports whether Trayo can now identify the company. Importing the same hostname again skips the existing account and does not update it. After the current run settles, start a new discovery for the corrected account IDs.

**Each blocked entry NAMES the accounts** in `accountIds` (the first 200 of them; `accountsAffected` is the true total), so a re-run can be scoped to exactly those rather than everything you sent.

Read events via `GET /v1/events?discoveryRunId={runId}`. Key behaviors: (1) Results deduplicate against workspace data—identical reruns return `eventsNew: 0` (success, not failure); (2) Send `Idempotency-Key` for retry safety; (3) Check `error` and `blockedSignals` even on 202—no events may follow if accounts are ineligible; (4) Use `people: "add"` to include relevant contacts; (5) `settledAt` marks final completion (search + event writing done), not `completedAt` alone. data.current_description:
**Required permissions:** `events:read`.

THE POLL. Call this until `settledAt` is non-null, then read the events that stand for the run's scope. `settledAt` and `status: completed` arrive together and mean the run is over in full: searched, and every event it produced written. From that moment the candidate and event counts are frozen and `GET /v1/events?discoveryRunId=` returns the complete scope: everything this run wrote, at any event date, plus the account × signal × lookback matches, including events an earlier run wrote. The counters remain about this execution and are not the size of that page — though a settled run paged to the end yields at least `eventsNew`, which one page need not. The same read before settlement returns what the run has written so far. There is no timer to wait out.

Two things NOT to poll on. `completedAt` marks only the first half, the search: it can be set while `status` is still `running`, because the events from that search are still being written. And do not watch `eventsNew` stop changing — a pause between two writes looks exactly like the end of a run and is not one. Read `error` even when `status` is `completed`.

**How long to wait.** `progress` says how many accounts are finished and, once there is enough data, `etaSeconds` and `estimatedSettleAt` estimate when the run settles. While the run is unsettled the response carries a `Retry-After` header (and `progress.retryAfterSeconds`): read the run again after that many seconds rather than on a fixed short timer.
data.summary_suggestion: Poll discovery run status until completion
data.description_suggestion: Retrieves the status and progress of a discovery run. **Required permissions:** `events:read`. Poll this endpoint until `settledAt` is non-null to determine when the run has completed both searching and writing all events. Returns run metadata including `status` (running/completed/failed), candidate and event counts, progress indicators (`etaSeconds`, `estimatedSettleAt`), and error details if applicable. Use `Retry-After` header or `progress.retryAfterSeconds` to determine polling interval. Do NOT poll on `completedAt` (marks only search completion, not event writing) or `eventsNew` (pauses between writes are indistinguishable from completion). After settlement, use `GET /v1/events?discoveryRunId={runId}` to retrieve all events produced by this run.

data.current_description:
**Required permissions:** `people:write`.

**A person is a name, a title, a note, an email, a LinkedIn username and a photo URL. That is the whole record you can WRITE.** Phone numbers are only ever found: `POST /v1/people/{id}/enrich` looks up an email and/or a phone and the results appear on the person as `email` (with `emailSource: "enrichment"`) and `phone`.

**`note` is where sourcing and confidence go.** It is free text you own — up to 1000 characters, no structure imposed, stored and returned verbatim and NEVER interpreted by Trayo: not parsed, not indexed, not searchable, not shown in the Trayo UI, and nothing in the product branches on it. `"sourced from LinkedIn, unverified, 2026-09-02"` is exactly the intended use. Set it here, change or clear it with `PATCH /v1/people/{id}`, read it back on every people route.

**Do not put any of that in `title`.** `title` is the job title, it is published, and humans and downstream systems read it as a job title — so a value like `"VP Sales (UNVERIFIED, sourced from LinkedIn)"` is a wrong job title for every reader of it, not an annotated one. That workaround is why `note` exists.

**LinkedIn and email are upsert keys.** A create that matches an existing person on either key updates that row with the fields you sent, makes it rep-visible, returns its existing `id`, and answers `200`. A new person answers `201`. WHERE Trayo looks depends on what you sent: with an `accountId` or a `company`, within THAT account only — the same human under two accounts (an advisor, a dual role) is two records and both are created. With neither, across your whole workspace, because you asked "do you have this person" and the answer must not depend on which account Trayo happens to attach them to. A person with neither key can never upsert. If LinkedIn and email point at two different people, the request is a `409` rather than merging those identities.

**`linkedinUrl` is a source for `linkedinUsername`, not a decoration.** Send either. With no `linkedinUsername`, the username is taken from the URL and stored, so a `POST /v1/find` contacts row keeps its LinkedIn identity when posted verbatim. A `linkedinUsername` you send always wins over the URL.

**For a new person, a LinkedIn identity also FILLS the fields you left empty.** A new row carrying one is looked up in Trayo's own profile mirror, and whatever it finds is used for `title` and `photoUrl` when you sent neither, and for the account link when you sent neither `accountId` nor `company` — so the response can carry a `title`, a `profileImageUrl` and an `accountId` you never supplied, and a company Trayo does not already have becomes a NEW account under the same name-only rule below. It never overwrites a value you DID send, and it is best-effort: a lookup that misses or takes too long creates the row exactly as you sent it rather than failing it. Supply the fields yourself to keep control of them; there is no other way to opt out. A strong-key upsert writes only fields you sent; it never copies these profile values onto the match.

Note `isRepVisible` on the response: it comes back `true`. Creating a person here counts as a deliberate human add, the same as adding one by hand in the app, so the record surfaces to reps. You cannot send the field and you cannot turn it off.

`accountId` and `company` are mutually exclusive ways to link the new person to an account — send at most one, or neither to create an unlinked person.

**Company auto-link.** `company: { name }` finds-or-creates the linked account by `name`, case-insensitive, within your workspace. A match reuses the existing account and `company.domain` is ignored. `company.domain` takes a bare host or a full website URL; the account is created at `https://<host>` either way, and a value that is not a usable hostname is refused — `validation_failed`, `param: "company.domain"`.

A company that does NOT already exist is created anyway — with an empty `url` when you sent no `company.domain`, so a name-only row still gets an account rather than being refused. Supply `company.domain` when you have one so the new account gets a real url. Look up whether an account already exists, and get its `id` for the `accountId` route, with `GET /v1/accounts?q=<company name>`.

data.current_summary: Find an email or phone for a person you describe
data.current_description:
**Required permissions:** `body.fields` includes `email`: `people:enrich_email`; `body.fields` includes `phone`: `people:enrich_phone`. All scopes for the selected fields are required. Omitting `body.fields` uses `["email"]` and requires `people:enrich_email`. Malformed values: no additional scopes; unknown fields add no scopes. Request validation still applies.

Give a person — their name, and their LinkedIn profile or where they work — and get their email back in the same response, and their phone as a lookup to poll. The person does not have to exist in your workspace, and this call does not create them: it is `POST /v1/people/{id}/enrich` with the person row taken out of the middle, for the case where you are still deciding whether someone is worth keeping.

**Email is synchronous.** Typically a few seconds, and the server gives up at 30 with `503 contact_lookup_failed`, so set your client timeout above that. Import the people you want afterwards with `POST /v1/people` (send the `email` you got back as the person's email).

**Phone is asynchronous.** Ask for it with `fields: ["phone"]` and the response is `202` with `phone.status: "pending"` and a `phone.lookupId`; collect it from `GET /v1/contacts/lookups/{lookupId}`. Phone lookups typically take one to two minutes, but can take up to four minutes. Email asked for in the same call is still answered inline, in the same response.

**What it costs.** One lookup per field when a search starts (a phone counts when it starts, so polling is free), counted against your plan's allowance for that field — email and phone have separate limits. A lookup here and a lookup on a person draw on the same allowance for the same field. Over the limit is `402 lookup_limit_reached` before any search starts. The response carries `quota`: the allowance left per field after this call, the same numbers `GET /v1/whoami` reports.

**Asking twice is free.** The workspace's answer for one identity is remembered — a month for a found address, a week for `not_found` — and a repeat request reads it: `source: "saved"`, no new lookup, and nothing counted against your allowance. So a retry after `not_found` costs nothing.

**A found address is not a verified owner.** `status: "found"` means a search returned the address and nothing suggests it belongs to someone else. `status: "unconfirmed"` means a search returned it but `email.identityConfidence` is `conflict`: the address is still in `value`, and a human should look before anyone sends to it. `email.identityConfidence` (`match`, `conflict` or `unknown`) says why. It compares the address against the `fullName` you sent, always, and against the `company.website` you sent, when you sent one. Include the known employer website even with a LinkedIn profile; without it, a matching name can produce `match` at the wrong employer. `match` does not prove mailbox ownership or current employment, and this field does not block sending.

**`not_found` is an answer.** The lookup finished without a value and returns `200`. A `503` means the question was never answered — nothing charged, nothing stored.

**Partial success is the contract.** When you ask for both fields and one fails because of a plan limit or a lookup error, the call still answers. That field reads `status: "failed"` with `error.code`, `error.retry` and `error.message`, exactly what an error response would have carried. The other field keeps its answer and its `lookupId`. Nothing is charged for a field that failed. The call itself fails only when every field you asked for did.

**What to send.** Include the LinkedIn profile when known to improve the chance of finding contact details. Otherwise, send the company website. A name alone returns `400`.

**Required permissions:** `accounts:write`.

Create up to 200 accounts in one call — the import path for bulk results (e.g. from `POST /v1/find`), where creating one account per HTTP call is the wrong shape. Every created account is assigned to the user your API key acts as, and starts becoming searchable, exactly like `POST /v1/accounts`. Read that route's description for what is and is not true of a new account; it applies to every row created here. Like that route, this call adds accounts only, never people.

**This call does not wait for the background work each new account needs.** That work is started without waiting for it, so 200 rows cost 200 inserts plus one website check that is capped at a few seconds; the accounts become searchable by `jobs` and `job_change` over the following minutes, and a discovery run tells you which are not ready yet rather than silently returning nothing for them.

**Each created row carries a prediction of which company it is.** Before answering, the websites of the created rows are checked together, and each row in `created` carries `identity`: `resolved` (with the company in `matchedCompany`), `uncertain` (several possible companies on that website, listed in `alternatives`), `not_found` (no company for that website: discovery will fail with `company_not_found`), or `pending` (no `url`, a `linkedinHandle` the website did not confirm, or the check did not answer in time; these are identified in the background, and a discovery run reports any that fail). Fix an `uncertain` or `not_found` account with `PATCH /v1/accounts/{id}` (its own website or its `linkedinHandle`), or delete it, before running discovery. `identity` is a prediction from the website: discovery runs its own match for each new account afterwards, and that match can land on a different company or on none. A discovery run lists any account it could not identify in `blockedSignals`; over MCP, `trayo_get_account_matches` reads the final result. Skipped rows carry none of this. These fields are on this response only, not on the account itself.

**Project a find result before posting it — it is not accepted verbatim.** A find company row carries `id`, `website`, `linkedinUrl`, `industry`, `headcount`, `hq`, `fundingStage`, `foundedYear`, `companyType`, `description`, `why`, `known`, `state` alongside `name` and `url`, this route accepts none of them, and an unprojected batch therefore lands EVERY row in `skipped` (the reason names the keys). The import that works:

```
curl -s .../v1/find -d '{"target":"companies","query":"..."}' | jq '{accounts: [.data[] | select(.state == "selectable" and .url) | {name, url}]}' \
  | curl -s .../v1/accounts/batch -H 'content-type: application/json' -d @-
```

The `select(.state == "selectable")` half matters as much as the projection: an `alreadyAdded` row would be skipped as a duplicate anyway.

**Partial success is the contract.** A malformed row, or one that collides with another row in the SAME batch or with an account you already have, is reported in `skipped` by its 0-based index and a reason — never as a request error. This response is always `200`, even if every row was skipped. Only a problem with the REQUEST itself fails the call, and an array over the 200-item cap is one of those: it ERRORS rather than clamping, unlike `POST /v1/find`'s `limit`.

Public REST and MCP usage is recorded without daily usage caps, workspace quota cutoffs or lookup quotas for now. Workspace request pacing still applies. **Dedup is best-effort, not a guarantee.** A row is a duplicate when its `url`'s hostname matches, lowercased and with a leading `www.` stripped (`https://acme.com` and `https://www.acme.com/careers` collide, and so does a stored value kept without a scheme, `acme.com`). Failing that, a row is a duplicate when its `linkedinHandle` matches — so a company you already have under a different domain (a rebrand, a regional TLD, an account whose `url` is empty) is still recognised. That comparison folds together every shape the handle is stored in: case, percent-encoding (`airbus%2Dhelicopters`), and a full company URL rather than the bare slug. Last, a row is a duplicate by `name`, case-insensitively, and how far that key reaches depends on what else the row carries. A row with NEITHER a `url` NOR a `linkedinHandle` has only its name, so it is matched against every account in your workspace, those with a website as well as those without — a name-only import is not created twice, and it attaches to the company you already have. A row that DOES carry a `url` or a handle and missed on it is matched by name only against an account that has NEITHER a usable website NOR a `linkedinHandle` — the only case where a name is the sole thing the two records share. Two accounts that each have a real website are never matched on name, so two different companies with the same name both land. The `reason` on the skip names WHICH of the three keys collided.

**A duplicate skip still attaches you to the account.** The account named by `existingId` is assigned to the user your key acts as, exactly as a created one is, so importing a company a teammate added already makes it eligible for your discovery runs. Importing a duplicate does not otherwise update the existing account; use `PATCH /v1/accounts/{id}` to correct its `name`, `url` or `linkedinHandle`.

This check happens in APPLICATION CODE — `Account.domain` has no unique database index, deliberately, because that migration needs a data backfill of its own. The consequence: two batches racing each other can both pass the duplicate check for the same key before either has committed, and both create an account. This endpoint cannot detect or prevent that race, there is no `Idempotency-Key` support here (unlike `POST /v1/discoveries`), and replaying the exact same request is not guaranteed to be a no-op. If your workflow cannot tolerate an occasional duplicate under concurrent imports, serialize your batch calls.

data.current_description:
**ASYNCHRONOUS.** Returns 202 immediately with a run whose `status` is `running` — nothing has been searched yet. Poll `GET /v1/discoveries/{runId}` until `settledAt` is non-null, then read the events that stand for its scope with `GET /v1/events?discoveryRunId={runId}`. `settledAt` is set when the run is final — searched AND every event written — and `status` reads `completed` or `failed` at the same instant. `candidatesScreened`, `candidatesMatched` and `eventsNew` are frozen execution counters; the scoped event page holds everything this run wrote — including events dated outside the lookback, as a job change dated by its start month can be — plus matching canonical events written by earlier runs.

**Re-running an identical discovery is safe.** Results deduplicate against everything already in the workspace, so the same accounts/signals/lookback typically returns `eventsNew: 0` the second time and creates no duplicate events. That is success.

**Idempotency:** send `Idempotency-Key` on every call you might retry. Repeating the same key with the byte-identical body returns the ORIGINAL run with the same `id`, without starting another search, but with its CURRENT state, not a frozen copy: if the original has since completed, the replay shows `status: completed` and real counts. The same key with a DIFFERENT body is a 409. Keys are not scoped to a time window in this version.

**A 202 does not guarantee events will follow.** If none of the requested accounts are eligible — every account must be assigned to a user, which accounts created via `POST /v1/accounts` always are — the run still returns 202 and then immediately reads `status: completed`, `eventsNew: 0`, with `error` explaining why. This is the single most likely way a first-time caller sees "no events": check `error` before assuming discovery is still running or that your signals match nothing.

You can use new accounts and signal keys immediately. Poll the same run until `settledAt` is set.

Public REST and MCP usage is recorded without daily usage caps, workspace quota cutoffs or lookup quotas for now. Workspace request pacing still applies. **People:** by default (`people: "none"`) a run adds no people to your workspace — its events come back with `people: []`. A `job_change` event still names the person who changed jobs; add them with `POST /v1/people` if you want them. Send `people: "add"` to have the people who matter to each event added to your workspace and listed on it.

Read `blockedSignals` before reporting an empty result. These outcomes apply to every signal type, including `news`. data.current_description:
**Required permissions:** `people:write`.

**A person is a name, a title, a note, an email, a LinkedIn username and a photo URL. That is the whole record you can WRITE.** Phone numbers are only ever found: `POST /v1/people/{id}/enrich` looks up an email and/or a phone and the results appear on the person as `email` (with `emailSource: "enrichment"`) and `phone`.

**`note` is where sourcing and confidence go.** It is free text you own — up to 1000 characters, no structure imposed, stored and returned verbatim and NEVER interpreted by Trayo: not parsed, not indexed, not searchable, not shown in the Trayo UI, and nothing in the product branches on it. `"sourced from LinkedIn, unverified, 2026-09-02"` is exactly the intended use. Set it here, change or clear it with `PATCH /v1/people/{id}`, read it back on every people route.

**Do not put any of that in `title`.** `title` is the job title, it is published, and humans and downstream systems read it as a job title — so a value like `"VP Sales (UNVERIFIED, sourced from LinkedIn)"` is a wrong job title for every reader of it, not an annotated one. That workaround is why `note` exists.

**LinkedIn and email are upsert keys.** A create that matches an existing person on either key updates that row with the fields you sent, makes it rep-visible, returns its existing `id`, and answers `200`. A new person answers `201`. WHERE Trayo looks depends on what you sent: with an `accountId` or a `company`, within THAT account only — the same human under two accounts (an advisor, a dual role) is two records and both are created. With neither, across your whole workspace, because you asked "do you have this person" and the answer must not depend on which account Trayo happens to attach them to. A person with neither key can never upsert. If LinkedIn and email point at two different people, the request is a `409` rather than merging those identities.

**`linkedinUrl` is a source for `linkedinUsername`, not a decoration.** Send either. With no `linkedinUsername`, the username is taken from the URL and stored, so a `POST /v1/find` contacts row keeps its LinkedIn identity when posted verbatim. A `linkedinUsername` you send always wins over the URL.

**For a new person, a LinkedIn identity also FILLS the fields you left empty.** A new row carrying one is looked up in Trayo's own profile mirror, and whatever it finds is used for `title` and `photoUrl` when you sent neither, and for the account link when you sent neither `accountId` nor `company` — so the response can carry a `title`, a `profileImageUrl` and an `accountId` you never supplied, and a company Trayo does not already have becomes a NEW account under the same name-only rule below. It never overwrites a value you DID send, and it is best-effort: a lookup that misses or takes too long creates the row exactly as you sent it rather than failing it. Supply the fields yourself to keep control of them; there is no other way to opt out. A strong-key upsert writes only fields you sent; it never copies these profile values onto the match.

Note `isRepVisible` on the response: it comes back `true`. Creating a person here counts as a deliberate human add, the same as adding one by hand in the app, so the record surfaces to reps. You cannot send the field and you cannot turn it off.

`accountId` and `company` are mutually exclusive ways to link the new person to an account — send at most one, or neither to create an unlinked person.

**Company auto-link.** `company: { name }` finds-or-creates the linked account by `name`, case-insensitive, within your workspace. A match reuses the existing account and `company.domain` is ignored. `company.domain` takes a bare host or a full website URL; the account is created at `https://<host>` either way, and a value that is not a usable hostname is refused — `validation_failed`, `param: "company.domain"`.

A company that does NOT already exist is created anyway — with an empty `url` when you sent no `company.domain`, so a name-only row still gets an account rather than being refused. Supply `company.domain` when you have one so the new account gets a real url. Look up whether an account already exists, and get its `id` for the `accountId` route, with `GET /v1/accounts?q=<company name>`.

data.current_summary: Find an email or phone for a person you describe
data.current_description:
**Required permissions:** `body.fields` includes `email`: `people:enrich_email`; `body.fields` includes `phone`: `people:enrich_phone`. All scopes for the selected fields are required. Omitting `body.fields` uses `["email"]` and requires `people:enrich_email`. Malformed values: no additional scopes; unknown fields add no scopes. Request validation still applies.

Give a person — their name, and their LinkedIn profile or where they work — and get their email back in the same response, and their phone as a lookup to poll. The person does not have to exist in your workspace, and this call does not create them: it is `POST /v1/people/{id}/enrich` with the person row taken out of the middle, for the case where you are still deciding whether someone is worth keeping.

**Email is synchronous.** Typically a few seconds, and the server gives up at 30 with `503 contact_lookup_failed`, so set your client timeout above that. Import the people you want afterwards with `POST /v1/people` (send the `email` you got back as the person's email).

**Phone is asynchronous.** Ask for it with `fields: ["phone"]` and the response is `202` with `phone.status: "pending"` and a `phone.lookupId`; collect it from `GET /v1/contacts/lookups/{lookupId}`. Phone lookups typically take one to two minutes, but can take up to four minutes. Email asked for in the same call is still answered inline, in the same response.

**What it costs.** One lookup per field when a search starts (a phone counts when it starts, so polling is free), counted against your plan's allowance for that field — email and phone have separate limits. A lookup here and a lookup on a person draw on the same allowance for the same field. Over the limit is `402 lookup_limit_reached` before any search starts. The response carries `quota`: the allowance left per field after this call, the same numbers `GET /v1/whoami` reports.

**Asking twice is free.** The workspace's answer for one identity is remembered — a month for a found address, a week for `not_found` — and a repeat request reads it: `source: "saved"`, no new lookup, and nothing counted against your allowance. So a retry after `not_found` costs nothing.

**A found address is not a verified owner.** `status: "found"` means a search returned the address and nothing suggests it belongs to someone else. `status: "unconfirmed"` means a search returned it but `email.identityConfidence` is `conflict`: the address is still in `value`, and a human should look before anyone sends to it. `email.identityConfidence` (`match`, `conflict` or `unknown`) says why. It compares the address against the `fullName` you sent, always, and against the `company.website` you sent, when you sent one. Include the known employer website even with a LinkedIn profile; without it, a matching name can produce `match` at the wrong employer. `match` does not prove mailbox ownership or current employment, and this field does not block sending.

**`not_found` is an answer.** The lookup finished without a value and returns `200`. A `503` means the question was never answered — nothing charged, nothing stored.

**Partial success is the contract.** When you ask for both fields and one fails because of a plan limit or a lookup error, the call still answers. That field reads `status: "failed"` with `error.code`, `error.retry` and `error.message`, exactly what an error response would have carried. The other field keeps its answer and its `lookupId`. Nothing is charged for a field that failed. The call itself fails only when every field you asked for did.

**What to send.** Include the LinkedIn profile when known to improve the chance of finding contact details. Otherwise, send the company website. A name alone returns `400`.

data.current_summary: Find companies similar to a list of seed companies
data.current_description:
**Required permissions:** `accounts:read`.

Send 1–50 companies by companyId, linkedinUrl, website or name, and a limit (default 100, maximum 500). companyId is an exact company dataset ID (number or numeric string), not a workspace account UUID. When supplied, it takes precedence; a missing ID is reported without trying other fields. Otherwise each company resolves by LinkedIn first, then its marketing website including redirects, then its name. Duplicate matched identities contribute once. No saved accounts are required. Optional hard filters minEmployees, maxEmployees, countries (ISO-2 codes or country names), regions and industries drop candidates outside them, including those with an unknown value for a filtered field unless includeUnknown is set; an employee bound replaces the seed size range.

Returns candidates sorted by similarity to the closest seed, with preliminary high/medium/low bands. Matched seeds and candidates include companyId for reuse in later searches. Check seeds for each matched identity and whether it contributed. Unmatched or unindexed seeds are reported and skipped. If none can contribute, companies is empty. A search failure returns 503. The seed companies themselves are excluded; other existing workspace accounts may appear.

Synchronous, read-only and unmetered. Allow more than 45 seconds for the client timeout. Returns up to limit candidates in one response, with no pagination. Import selected results using POST /v1/accounts/batch.

data.current_summary: Rank the competitors of one company
data.current_description:
**Required permissions:** `accounts:read`.

Send one company ({ self: true } for your own workspace, or companyId / linkedinUrl / website / name) and get back a ranked roster, default 15 and at most 50. Rank 1 is your first pin when you send pins, else the category incumbent, else the closest match on product and buyer. Candidates are drawn from companies similar to the subject plus companies named while the roster is generated; each is judged direct, adjacent or not a competitor, with 0..100 product and ICP alignment.

The roster is stored per workspace and subject. A repeat call with the same pins and an equal or smaller cap returns the stored roster (reused: true) and does not generate a new one, so a changed positioning has no effect until you send refresh: true. Sending pins replaces the stored pins for that subject; a new roster is generated when the pin set changes. Sending pins stores them for the workspace under the same accounts:read scope. Synchronous. Generation typically takes 10 to 25 seconds; allow 45 seconds for the client timeout.

data.current_description:
**Required permissions:** `accounts:write`.

An account is a name, an optional URL and an optional LinkedIn handle. That is the whole record — see `AccountDto` for what reads back. `name` is the only required field: an account you have no website for is created with `url: null` rather than refused, the same way `POST /v1/people` treats a `company` with no `domain`. Send `url` whenever you have it — it is this route's deduplication key. Supply `linkedinHandle` whenever you know the company page: use the bare handle (for example `stripe`), not the full LinkedIn URL. It is the strongest way to identify the company and takes precedence over the website and name.

You can start discovery immediately after creating an account. These outcomes apply to every signal type, including `news`. While a run is active, keep polling the same run. `account_not_ready` means Trayo could not search the account this time. After the run settles, retry the affected account IDs. `company_not_found` means Trayo could not identify the company from the supplied details. For `company_not_found`, check the named accounts before starting another discovery. If an identity is wrong, send the correct `linkedinHandle` with `trayo_update_account` over MCP, or with `PATCH /v1/accounts/{id}` and a workspace API key over REST. When no handle is known, send a corrected website `url` instead. Both need `accounts:write`. `trayo_update_account` also reports whether Trayo can now identify the company. Importing the same hostname again skips the existing account and does not update it. After the current run settles, start a new discovery for the corrected account IDs.

Public REST and MCP usage is recorded without daily usage caps, workspace quota cutoffs or lookup quotas for now. Workspace request pacing still applies. **This call adds the account only, never people.** Finding people and adding them are separate steps: search with `POST /v1/find` as many times as you need, then add the people you chose with `POST /v1/people/batch`.

To attach people to future events, first set the workspace stakeholder definition with `PATCH /v1/workspace`, then start discovery with `people: "add"`. This definition does not add people to older events.

**A `POST /v1/find` company row is NOT postable verbatim.** Its `id`, `website`, `linkedinUrl`, `industry`, `headcount`, `hq`, `fundingStage`, `foundedYear`, `companyType`, `description`, `why`, `known`, `state` fields are all refused with `validation_failed`, and the message names the offending keys. They are refused rather than accepted-and-dropped on purpose: these company details cannot be saved through this route. Select the accepted fields first: `jq '.data[] | select(.state == "selectable" and .url) | {name, url}'`.

data.current_description:
**Required permissions:** `accounts:write`.

Create up to 200 accounts in one call — the import path for bulk results (e.g. from `POST /v1/find`), where creating one account per HTTP call is the wrong shape. Every created account is assigned to the user your API key acts as, and starts becoming searchable, exactly like `POST /v1/accounts`. Read that route's description for what is and is not true of a new account; it applies to every row created here. Like that route, this call adds accounts only, never people.

**This call does not wait for the background work each new account needs.** That work is started without waiting for it, so 200 rows cost 200 inserts plus one website check that is capped at a few seconds; the accounts become searchable by `jobs` and `job_change` over the following minutes, and a discovery run tells you which are not ready yet rather than silently returning nothing for them.

**Each created row carries a prediction of which company it is.** Before answering, the websites of the created rows are checked together, and each row in `created` carries `identity`: `resolved` (with the company in `matchedCompany`), `uncertain` (several possible companies on that website, listed in `alternatives`), `not_found` (no company for that website: discovery will fail with `company_not_found`), or `pending` (no `url`, a `linkedinHandle` the website did not confirm, or the check did not answer in time; these are identified in the background, and a discovery run reports any that fail). Fix an `uncertain` or `not_found` account with `PATCH /v1/accounts/{id}` (its own website or its `linkedinHandle`), or delete it, before running discovery. `identity` is a prediction from the website: discovery runs its own match for each new account afterwards, and that match can land on a different company or on none. A discovery run lists any account it could not identify in `blockedSignals`; over MCP, `trayo_get_account_matches` reads the final result. Skipped rows carry none of this. These fields are on this response only, not on the account itself.

**Project a find result before posting it — it is not accepted verbatim.** A find company row carries `id`, `website`, `linkedinUrl`, `industry`, `headcount`, `hq`, `fundingStage`, `foundedYear`, `companyType`, `description`, `why`, `known`, `state` alongside `name` and `url`, this route accepts none of them, and an unprojected batch therefore lands EVERY row in `skipped` (the reason names the keys). The import that works:

```
curl -s .../v1/find -d '{"target":"companies","query":"..."}' | jq '{accounts: [.data[] | select(.state == "selectable" and .url) | {name, url}]}' \
  | curl -s .../v1/accounts/batch -H 'content-type: application/json' -d @-
```

The `select(.state == "selectable")` half matters as much as the projection: an `alreadyAdded` row would be skipped as a duplicate anyway.

**Partial success is the contract.** A malformed row, or one that collides with another row in the SAME batch or with an account you already have, is reported in `skipped` by its 0-based index and a reason — never as a request error. This response is always `200`, even if every row was skipped. Only a problem with the REQUEST itself fails the call, and an array over the 200-item cap is one of those: it ERRORS rather than clamping, unlike `POST /v1/find`'s `limit`.

Public REST and MCP usage is recorded without daily usage caps, workspace quota cutoffs or lookup quotas for now. Workspace request pacing still applies. **Dedup is best-effort, not a guarantee.** A row is a duplicate when its `url`'s hostname matches, lowercased and with a leading `www.` stripped (`https://acme.com` and `https://www.acme.com/careers` collide, and so does a stored value kept without a scheme, `acme.com`). Failing that, a row is a duplicate when its `linkedinHandle` matches — so a company you already have under a different domain (a rebrand, a regional TLD, an account whose `url` is empty) is still recognised. That comparison folds together every shape the handle is stored in: case, percent-encoding (`airbus%2Dhelicopters`), and a full company URL rather than the bare slug. Last, a row is a duplicate by `name`, case-insensitively, and how far that key reaches depends on what else the row carries. A row with NEITHER a `url` NOR a `linkedinHandle` has only its name, so it is matched against every account in your workspace, those with a website as well as those without — a name-only import is not created twice, and it attaches to the company you already have. A row that DOES carry a `url` or a handle and missed on it is matched by name only against an account that has NEITHER a usable website NOR a `linkedinHandle` — the only case where a name is the sole thing the two records share. Two accounts that each have a real website are never matched on name, so two different companies with the same name both land. The `reason` on the skip names WHICH of the three keys collided.

**A duplicate skip still attaches you to the account.** The account named by `existingId` is assigned to the user your key acts as, exactly as a created one is, so importing a company a teammate added already makes it eligible for your discovery runs. Importing a duplicate does not otherwise update the existing account; use `PATCH /v1/accounts/{id}` to correct its `name`, `url` or `linkedinHandle`.

This check happens in APPLICATION CODE — `Account.domain` has no unique database index, deliberately, because that migration needs a data backfill of its own. The consequence: two batches racing each other can both pass the duplicate check for the same key before either has committed, and both create an account. This endpoint cannot detect or prevent that race, there is no `Idempotency-Key` support here (unlike `POST /v1/discoveries`), and replaying the exact same request is not guaranteed to be a no-op. If your workflow cannot tolerate an occasional duplicate under concurrent imports, serialize your batch calls.
